shelf_items.name: Moseley's sham surgery study for knee osteoarthritis
shelf_items.what_it_found: Arthroscopic debridement and lavage were no better than sham surgery (incision only) for pain relief; placebo effect accounted for all improvement.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Randomized controlled trial (2002, New England Journal of Medicine), replicated by other sham surgery studies (e.g., vertebroplasty, subacromial decompression).
shelf_items.why_buried: Threatened the surgical-pharmaceutical model; funding for sham surgery trials is scarce; results often ignored in clinical guidelines.
shelf_items.current_status: Still cited but underutilized; sham surgery trials remain rare due to ethical and funding barriers.

shelf_items.name: Fabrizio Benedetti's placebo research program
shelf_items.what_it_found: Placebo effects are real neurobiological phenomena (e.g., endogenous opioid release, dopamine activation) that can mimic drug effects; open-label placebos work even when patients know they are placebos.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Multiple controlled experiments, neuroimaging studies, and clinical trials (e.g., open-label placebo for irritable bowel syndrome, chronic pain).
shelf_items.why_buried: Placebo effects undermine the drug-specific efficacy narrative; pharmaceutical industry has little incentive to study non-drug interventions.
shelf_items.current_status: Growing recognition in academic circles, but still marginalized in mainstream clinical practice and drug approval processes.

shelf_items.name: Irving Kirsch's analysis of antidepressant efficacy
shelf_items.what_it_found: Antidepressants (SSRIs) show clinically insignificant benefits over placebo for mild to moderate depression; the drug-placebo difference is largely due to side effects breaking blinding.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Meta-analyses of FDA trial data (2002, 2008, 2014), reanalyses of published and unpublished trials.
shelf_items.why_buried: Directly challenged the blockbuster antidepressant market; Kirsch faced ad hominem attacks and funding cuts.
shelf_items.current_status: Controversial but increasingly supported by subsequent meta-analyses; still dismissed by many psychiatrists.

shelf_items.name: John Ioannidis's work on research integrity and drug trials
shelf_items.what_it_found: Most published research findings are false; drug trials are systematically biased by industry funding, selective reporting, and small sample sizes.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Landmark 2005 paper 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'; empirical reanalyses of thousands of trials.
shelf_items.why_buried: Threatens the entire evidence hierarchy; Ioannidis faced resistance from journal editors and industry-funded researchers.
shelf_items.current_status: Highly cited but slow to change practice; replication crisis acknowledged but not resolved.

shelf_items.name: Ted Kaptchuk's open-label placebo studies
shelf_items.what_it_found: Placebos work even when patients are told they are receiving a placebo (open-label placebo); effects are not just 'expectation' but involve conditioning and ritual.
shelf_items.evidence_strength: Randomized trials for IBS, chronic pain, migraine, and allergic rhinitis; replicated by multiple independent groups.
shelf_items.why_buried: Challenges the need for deception in placebo controls; pharmaceutical industry cannot patent open-label placebos.
shelf_items.current_status: Growing acceptance in academic medicine; still not integrated into standard care.
